shared_context.statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 2 and let g be an integer with g >= 0. Define K_{m,g} to be the set of all tuples x = (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) of positive integers such that x satisfies the Kunz inequalities for multiplicity m, namely: for all i,j in {1,...,m-1}, if i + j < m then x_i + x_j >= x_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then x_i + x_j + 1 >= x_{i+j-m}, and such that x_1 + ... + x_{m-1} = g. Then N(m,g), the number of numerical semigroups of multiplicity m and genus g, is equal to the cardinality of K_{m,g}.

payload.statement_nl: Let S be a numerical semigroup, meaning a subset S of the nonnegative integers that contains 0, is closed under addition, and has finite complement. Assume its multiplicity is m, meaning m >= 2 is the least positive element of S. For each r in {1,...,m-1}, let x_r be the least positive integer q such that q m + r belongs to S. Then the genus of S, that is, the number of nonnegative integers not belonging to S, is x_1 + ... + x_{m-1}.

result_payload.proof_nl:
Let S be a numerical semigroup, and let m be its multiplicity, so m is the least positive element of S and m>=2. For each r in {1,...,m-1}, define
x_r := min{ q in Z_{>=1} : qm+r in S }.
We must prove that genus(S) = sum_{r=1}^{m-1} x_r.

First we justify that each x_r is well-defined. Fix r in {1,...,m-1}. Since S has finite complement in Z_{>=0}, only finitely many nonnegative integers fail to belong to S. Among the infinitely many integers of the form qm+r with q>=1, at least one must therefore lie in S. Hence the set { q>=1 : qm+r in S } is nonempty. Being a nonempty set of positive integers, it has a least element, namely x_r.

Now fix r in {1,...,m-1}. By definition of x_r, we have:
- x_r m + r belongs to S;
- for every integer q with 1<=q<x_r, qm+r does not belong to S.
Also r itself does not belong to S, because 0<r<m and m is the least positive element of S. Therefore the integers in the residue class r modulo m that are not in S are at least
r, m+r, 2m+r, ..., (x_r-1)m+r.
These are exactly x_r numbers, corresponding to q=0,1,...,x_r-1.

We next show that there are no further gaps in this residue class. Let q>=x_r. Since x_r m + r is in S and m is in S, and S is closed under addition, we get
qm+r = (x_r m+r) + (q-x_r)m in S,
because (q-x_r)m is a nonnegative multiple of m and hence lies in S (indeed m in S and repeated addition gives km in S for every k>=0, with 0 in S as well). Thus every integer congruent to r mod m with quotient q>=x_r belongs to S.

So for each fixed r in {1,...,m-1}, the gaps of S in the residue class r modulo m are exactly
r, m+r, 2m+r, ..., (x_r-1)m+r,
and hence there are exactly x_r such gaps.

Now consider the residue class 0 modulo m. Since 0 is in S and m is in S, closure under addition shows that every nonnegative multiple of m belongs to S. Hence there are no gaps congruent to 0 mod m.

Therefore the complement Z_{>=0}\S is the disjoint union, over r=1,...,m-1, of the x_r gaps in residue class r modulo m. Since every nonnegative integer has a unique residue modulo m, these classes are disjoint and cover all nonzero residues. It follows that

genus(S) = #(Z_{>=0}\S) = sum_{r=1}^{m-1} x_r.

This is exactly the claimed formula.
result_payload.proof_summary: For each residue class r=1,...,m-1 mod m, finiteness of the complement guarantees existence of a least x_r>=1 with x_r m+r in S. Because m is the least positive element of S, the numbers r, m+r, ..., (x_r-1)m+r are not in S, while closure under addition with m implies every q m+r with q>=x_r is in S. Thus there are exactly x_r gaps in residue class r, and there are no gaps in residue class 0 since all multiples of m lie in S. Summing over residues gives genus(S)=sum_{r=1}^{m-1} x_r.

If m is in a submonoid S of Z_{>=0}, then every nonnegative multiple of m is in S by repeated addition.
